I'll give a different explanation, one the helped me understand the problem better.

Lets say that, instead of 3 prisoners, there are 2^24 prisoners, one for each hexadecimal color code. One prisoner randomly selected will die. Prisoner 0x000000 is worried he will die, and so asks the guard if he's going to die. The guard replies that every prisoner except 0x000000 and 0xAF273C are certain to survive. At the start, there is a 1/2^24 chance that 0x000000 was going to die, and a 2^24-1/2^24 chance that somebody else was going to die. If it truly was 0x000000 who was going to die, then a random other prisoner would be picked as the other execution candidate. But if it was any other prisoner, which it almost certainly is, then all of the people who live would be removed from the options and only poor prisoner 0xAF273C would remain. So there are 2^24-1 different ways that it could be the other person, and only 1 way that it could be the asker who is executed.

Counterintuitive? Certainly. Incorrect? No.

They're both valid interpretations of the same problem. It doesn't change the outcome.

We can broadly separate outcomes into two categories - the asker dies, or somebody else dies. If we are told that a specific non-asker prisoner is going to live, that tells us no new information to determine which outcome we get, since the guard will specifically choose somebody who was not chosen to die. This means that the same probability of n-1/n of the death being somebody other than the asker is going to be split across n-2 people instead of n-1 people.

Let's go back to prisoners 0x000000 through 0xFFFFFF, with the change that this time the guard tells 0x000000 that 0x231CD5 will survive. If 0x000000 was going to die, then the guard would have picked a random person who was going to live and told 0x000000 about the survivor. If 0x000000 was going to live, then the guard would just pick one of the 2^24-2 prisoners who aren't asking questions or going to die. There is still 1 "dead" outcome and 2^24-1 "alive" outcomes.

If the guard had answered the question, and then randomly selected the dead prisoner, taking his answer into account, then 0x000000 should have kept his mouth shut. But the dead prisoner was predetermined.

Isn't the "sleight of hand" in the rules that define what the guard is allowed to tell the green prisoner?

When green is told "orange will survive," if you're a normal human being (or Twilek) who does not know the rules that govern the guard's behavior, this only gives you enough info to assume 50% odds that it's either green or pink who will die.

But if you somehow know the rules that the guard is subjected to, then when the guard says "orange will survive," there is now more info encoded in that statement. From knowing the rules, the guard's statement carries additional implications compared to not knowing the rules (@2:28 in the video), and thus, when he tells green about orange surviving, this now has implications that we can reason about, which rules out several scenarios that we now can exclude (because if they happened, the guard would not have been able to say "orange survived," so we now know that these scenarios cannot occur).

I find that these probability problems play fast and loose with perspective in terms of presentation, which I do not like. The trick is to realize you're not the prisoner, and you do know about the rules that bind the guard's behavior, and thus have extra information that the prisoners don't not have, which further removes uncertainty, which by definition narrows down the probability.

Orange should not have been able to explain it to green, because why would orange know the rules of what the guard is allowed to say?
